clinicalPearls: Typically presents as a rapidly enlarging goitre or neck mass, often with compressive symptoms, in an older patient with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis
Almost always a non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or a marginal-zone (MALT) lymphoma arising in the setting of autoimmune thyroiditis
Chronic autoimmune inflammation in Hashimoto thyroiditis provides the lymphoid tissue from which MALT lymphoma can develop, so a history of hypothyroidism and positive thyroid antibodies is common

Because treatment is chemotherapy and radiotherapy rather than surgery, obtaining an adequate tissue diagnosis is critical and often needs core or open biopsy with flow cytometry, as aspiration may not suffice
May clinically mimic anaplastic carcinoma, but immunophenotyping distinguishes lymphoid from epithelial malignancy and carries a far better prognosis
Compressive features such as stridor, dysphagia, or hoarseness can develop quickly and require prompt airway assessment
Staging and management follow lymphoma principles, so haematology-oncology involvement and systemic assessment are essential
reference.pathophysiology: Primary thyroid lymphoma is a non-Hodgkin B-cell malignancy arising within the thyroid, almost invariably against a background of chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis. Persistent autoimmune stimulation recruits and expands intrathyroidal lymphoid tissue, and acquired genetic changes in this population can give rise to a clonal marginal-zone (MALT) lymphoma or transform into an aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The proliferating lymphoid cells rapidly efface and expand the gland, producing a fast-growing mass and compressive symptoms, but the disease responds to lymphoma-directed chemotherapy and radiotherapy rather than to thyroidectomy.
additionalDifferentials: Poorly differentiated or medullary thyroid carcinoma
Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia of the thyroid
Secondary or systemic lymphoma involving the thyroid
additionalInvestigations: Core needle or open biopsy with histology, immunohistochemistry, and flow cytometry for definitive diagnosis
Thyroid autoantibodies and thyroid function, given the strong association with Hashimoto thyroiditis
Neck ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging to define extent and compression
Systemic staging imaging such as CT and functional imaging per lymphoma protocols
Bone marrow assessment and lactate dehydrogenase as part of lymphoma staging
Airway assessment including laryngoscopy when compressive symptoms are present
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging mass with stridor or airway compromise requiring urgent assessment
New dysphagia or hoarseness from compression or invasion
Systemic B symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss indicating aggressive lymphoma
Superior vena cava obstruction from bulky mediastinal extension
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good and far better than for anaplastic carcinoma, particularly for localised MALT lymphoma; aggressive diffuse large B-cell histology, advanced stage, and extrathyroidal spread reduce response and survival.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing lymphoma as anaplastic carcinoma and thereby denying potentially curative lymphoma therapy
Relying on aspiration cytology alone, which may be insufficient to subtype lymphoma without flow cytometry or core biopsy
Proceeding to thyroidectomy for a disease that is treated medically
Overlooking an underlying Hashimoto thyroiditis that provides the diagnostic context
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Treat aggressive diffuse large B-cell histology with rituximab-based immunochemotherapy (an anthracycline-containing regimen) combined with involved-site radiotherapy rather than thyroidectomy
Treat localised marginal-zone (MALT) lymphoma with radiotherapy, with rituximab as an option, reserving surgery for diagnosis only
Secure an adequate tissue diagnosis by core or open biopsy with immunophenotyping and flow cytometry before starting treatment
Assess and protect the airway urgently when compressive stridor, dysphagia or hoarseness develops, using corticosteroids and airway support as needed
Replace thyroid hormone for the coexisting Hashimoto hypothyroidism and provide supportive care through chemotherapy
Stage and manage through a haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team, with post-treatment surveillance for relapse
